title: T20 Cricket Has Changed… Are We Still Speaking the Same Old Language?
subtitle: Why understanding the modern T20 demands a shift in perspective.
description: Why understanding the modern T20 demands a shift in perspective.
blocks: June 29, 2024. From the Barbados pavilion, Shivam Dube was walking out to bat in his first-ever World Cup final. The crowd had gone quiet. India, batting first, had slipped into what felt like a swamp. Quinton de Kock’s direct hit had run out Axar Patel just when he was trying to push the run rate. Even inside the dressing room, there was silence. And in T20, that kind of silence is dangerous.
The scoreboard did not look special. It felt like India would somehow crawl to 155 or 160 in the remaining overs. Shivam Dube was talking to himself.
“My job is not to play a big innings. My job is to bring the game back to life.”
At that moment, he was not just a batter. He was speaking the **language** of T20 cricket.

India eventually scored 176. The highest total ever in a T20 World Cup final. Dube made 27 off 16 balls at a strike rate of 168.75. Among Indian batters, his strike rate was the highest, minimum 10 runs. Yet on the scorecard, that innings does not stand out. With time, it is forgotten.
But that is not the fans’ fault.
The real question is this. Even though T20 belongs to the same family as Test cricket, are they really the same?

*In Tests, the scorecard is a mirror of the story. 
In T20, that does not always apply.*
In T20, when matters more than how much. T20 is teaching us a new language. **The only question is, are we ready to listen?**

In the early days of T20, everything felt unclear. No one knew what to expect. No one knew how to build a team. If you look at the squads from the first IPL season, it becomes obvious. There was no clear structure, no defined roles. Just big international names. Many of them were not suited for the format at all. Slowly, teams across the world understood that this game is completely different. The focus shifted from fast bowlers to spinners because across phases their economy rates were lower.
In Tests, the basic idea is simple. You cannot win without taking 20 wickets. So in the beginning, even T20 teams focused heavily on wickets. But soon it became clear that something was different.

In Tests, the value of a wicket is roughly the same in any over. 
In T20, the value of a wicket drops sharply.

A wicket in the first over is worth of around **12** runs. 
A wicket in the final over is worth just **2**.

Because of this, bowlers started focusing more on controlling runs than on chasing wickets. Mystery spinners became extremely valuable. Bowlers who could take the ball away from both right and left handers. Every player’s role became sharper. For example, as spinners grew in importance, so did spin hitters such as Shivam Dube. In the future, their value will only rise.

Both batters and bowlers evolved, but in different ways. Batters started using parts of the field that once seemed impossible. They stopped playing the ball and started playing the field. That change transformed bowling as well. Today, the best ball is not the one taught in traditional coaching manuals. It is the ball the batter does not expect or does not want.

Some franchises decoded their home conditions brilliantly. That is how T20 dynasties like **Mumbai Indians** and **Chennai Super Kings** were built. In the last T20 World Cup, India selected four spinners with different skill sets keeping Caribbean conditions in mind. They benefited from it fully.

At first, teams focused on reducing dot balls and rotating strike. But in T20, that thinking was fundamentally flawed. IPL 2024 shattered that belief when SRH chased 166 against LSG in just 58 balls. After the match, KL Rahul said, “I am lost for words.” For teams that had not understood the importance of boundary hitting, that was a painful lesson. Today, LSG’s top three attack from the **very first ball.**

For a bowler, it does not matter whether he gets a wicket. If he has not conceded a boundary, that itself is a win. We can sense all these changes while watching the match. But when we try to talk about them, the right words do not come. The scoreboard does not tell the whole story. T20 keeps reminding us of that.
That is why T20 demands a new perspective. A new vocabulary. A new language. Only then can we truly enjoy this format.
T20 initially inherited players, tactics and techniques from Test and ODI cricket. But in terms of strategy, the game evolved rapidly. The problem is that the language did not evolve with it.
The old vocabulary struggles to express the subtle shifts and decisive moments within a T20 match. Cricket’s language is excellent at describing individual performances.
But T20 is the most team focused format.
We need to identify and name the subtle elements and strategies at the heart of a T20 match. Only then can we understand and truly see them.
And this is not just theory.
Sometimes, in one match, in one moment, T20 speaks its own language right there on the field.
Let us return to Barbados once again.
Look at that scorecard carefully. 27 runs off 16 balls. The numbers do not say much. But ask a different question.
“How much did those 16 balls shift the future of the match?”
The table below shows how much each Indian batter increased the team’s **Win Probability** in the final.
When you look at that table, one thing becomes clear. Right after Axar Patel, who stands second on that list?
That is when you understand something. Some innings do not look big on the scorecard. But they bring a slipping match back to life. That is T20.

It does not always teach you to look at big numbers. It teaches you to recognize moments. That is why some T20 innings appear small statistically, but are enormous in the story of the match. Next time you watch a T20 game, maybe you will notice something different. Maybe you will remember that T20 is speaking its own language. If you understand that language, not just the match but the drama, the joy and the beauty will feel new.
**Now the only question left is this. Are we ready to listen?**
If this piece made you look at T20 differently, tell me what moment changed the game for you.

Not the biggest score. Not the loudest innings. 
The moment that quietly shifted everything.
If you believe T20 needs a new vocabulary, share this with someone who still judges matches only by the scorecard.
